Max Verstappen topped the timesheets during the opening practice hour at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, the Red Bull man setting the pace ahead of George Russell and Isack Hadjar.

Franco Colapinto led the pack out as the session got underway at 1230 local time, the Alpine racer one of a small number to sport the soft tyres while the majority of the field bolted on the medium compound for their first laps.

Verstappen – the last driver to win in Malaysia back in 2017 – had gone fastest at the 15-minute mark, while second-placed Russell seemed to be enjoying the challenge of mastering Sepang, the Briton radioing in: “This track is very cool.”

Meanwhile Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto commented on the high temperatures amid hot and humid conditions.

# FP1: Verstappen leads Russell and Hadjar during first practice at Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia

Red Bull's Max Verstappen set the pace during first practice at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Oct 02, 2026 5:50am UTC

![KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA - OCTOBER 02:  Max Verstappen of the Netherlands driving the (3) Oracle Red](https://media.formula1.com/image/upload/t_16by9Centre/c_lfill,w_3392/q_auto/v1740000001/trackside-images/2026/F1_Grand_Prix_of_Bahrain_in_Malaysia___Practice/2298168151.webp)

Max Verstappen topped the timesheets during the opening practice hour at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, the Red Bull man setting the pace ahead of George Russell and Isack Hadjar.

With the Sepang International Circuit having last hosted an F1 event back in 2017, many drivers on the grid had not previously experienced the Malaysian track – meaning that Friday’s first practice offered a valuable initial opportunity to get to grips with the venue.

Franco Colapinto led the pack out as the session got underway at 1230 local time, the Alpine racer one of a small number to sport the soft tyres while the majority of the field bolted on the medium compound for their first laps.

Another driver to use the soft rubber was Arvid Lindblad, with the Racing Bulls driver likely to start from the back of the grid on Sunday after the team reported that he would take on a fifth power unit this weekend.

Verstappen – the last driver to win in Malaysia back in 2017 – had gone fastest at the 15-minute mark, while second-placed Russell seemed to be enjoying the challenge of mastering Sepang, the Briton radioing in: “This track is very cool.”

Russell was followed by Kimi Antonelli on the timesheets, with Mercedes running an upgrade for the event as well as sporting a special livery in tribute to their title partner PETRONAS. Meanwhile Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto commented on the high temperatures amid hot and humid conditions.

Elsewhere, the McLaren drivers were each running a different rear wing, with the team hoping for a better weekend after a difficult end to their race last time out in Azerbaijan.

As the session moved into the final quarter, some drivers – including Russell and Antonelli – returned to the medium tyres. The latter looked to be pushing, as replays showed the championship leader having a wide moment out on track.

Amid further laps going on the board in the closing stages – as well as something of a mini race between Esteban Ocon and Carlos Sainz – it was Verstappen who remained on top when the chequered flag fell, followed by Russell and the other Red Bull of Hadjar.

## Summary

- Verstappen won the last F1 race at Sepang, on 1 October 2017.
- The 2026 cars use active aerodynamics and place much greater demands on electrical energy management.
- Teams must learn how this generation of cars and tyres behaves at Sepang during Friday practice.

When Formula 1 last raced at Sepang, Max Verstappen drove a Red Bull to victory ahead of Lewis Hamilton and Daniel Ricciardo. The date was 1 October 2017. Nine years later, the circuit returns to the calendar on 2–4 October 2026 as the venue for the **Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia**.

The name of the event is unusual, but the larger sporting question is what teams can learn from a circuit they have not visited with any of their current cars. Sepang still asks drivers to negotiate long straights, heavy braking, fast changes of direction, heat and humidity. The machinery responding to those demands has changed substantially.

A lap time or strategy sheet from 2017 offers historical context. It cannot tell a team how much electrical energy its 2026 car will have available at the end of a straight, how its active aerodynamics will affect the next braking zone or how the current tyres will perform over a race stint.

## What is different from F1’s last visit to Malaysia?

| Area | Sepang in 2017 | Sepang in 2026 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Race | Malaysian Grand Prix | Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia |
| Last winner / current reference | Verstappen won for Red Bull | The 2026 competitive order will be established in practice |
| Cars | Built to the 2017 aerodynamic rules | Shorter, narrower 2026 cars with active aerodynamics |
| Power units | Earlier generation of turbo hybrids | Greater electrical contribution and a different energy-management challenge |
| Wheels | 13-inch specification | 18-inch specification with narrower 2026 tyres |
| Teams | Ten teams | Eleven teams, following Cadillac’s arrival |
| Race distance | 56 laps | 56 laps |

## The 2026 power unit changes the question on Sepang’s straights

Sepang has two long straights connected by a slow final hairpin. In 2017, acceleration, aerodynamic drag and the performance of the turbo-hybrid power unit shaped a car’s speed through that section. Those factors still matter, but the 2026 regulations give electrical deployment a much larger role.

The new power units are designed around a roughly equal split between combustion and electrical power. Drivers can harvest energy under braking and through other phases of a lap, then deploy it where it is most useful. At Sepang, teams must establish how much energy they can recover through the braking zones and how to spend it across the circuit’s straights without compromising another part of the lap. The FIA also introduced active aerodynamics to work with the new power-unit concept.

That makes Friday more than an exercise in finding a qualifying setup. Engineers need to compare the expected energy profile from simulations with what happens on track, particularly as tyre wear, traffic and changing conditions alter the way a driver completes the lap. **GRANDE PRÊMIO** has examined [why Sepang poses a different test from Baku](https://grandepremio.com/en/f1/) for the 2026 cars; the first practice sessions will provide the evidence that simulations cannot.

## Tyres offer another break with 2017

The cars that raced at Sepang in 2017 used 13-inch wheels. Formula 1 moved to 18-inch wheels in 2022, and the 2026 tyres are narrower than those used immediately before the latest regulation change. It is therefore unsafe to carry a 2017 tyre-life estimate straight into this weekend’s strategy.

Pirelli has selected **C2, C3 and C4** for Sepang: hard, medium and soft respectively. That is a different selection from the softer C3–C5 range chosen for Baku and Singapore. Long runs in practice should help establish how the three compounds respond to the Malaysian circuit and whether the conditions support more than one competitive race strategy.

Weather can change that work quickly. A dry practice session provides useful information about degradation and cooling; rain would instead bring a different set of decisions about tyres, visibility and track conditions. Neither outcome should be assumed before the cars run.

## Some drivers know Sepang. The 2026 field does not know it together

Verstappen has a winning memory of Sepang. Hamilton finished second to him in 2017, while Fernando Alonso, Carlos Sainz, Sergio Pérez and several other current drivers also raced there during Formula 1’s previous Malaysian run. Many of their present rivals have never competed in a Formula 1 Grand Prix at the circuit.

Experience helps a driver recognise braking points, changes in grip and the physical demands of the venue. It does not provide a direct setup for a 2026 car. Teams also have new driver pairings, different technical groups and, in Cadillac’s case, an entirely new entrant since the last Malaysian race.

The 2017 result is therefore a useful marker for the story of F1 at Sepang, rather than a prediction for Sunday. Friday’s sessions will show which teams have arrived closest to a workable answer. FP1 begins at **12:30 local time on 2 October**, followed by FP2 at 16:00. Qualifying is on Saturday and the 56-lap race starts at 15:00 local time on Sunday.

## F1 today: FAQ

### Why did F1 cars lose power before the Bahrain GP in Malaysia?

The FIA identified a combination of low engine speed, low grip, wet-weather energy management settings and Sepang’s sector configuration. It distributed a software update before the race and announced a full review with teams and power unit manufacturers.

### Can Kimi Antonelli win the F1 championship in Singapore?

No. Antonelli leads George Russell by **84 points**, but even a Singapore Sprint and Grand Prix double would not secure the title. **Austin on 25 October is his earliest possible opportunity**, depending on his results and those of the remaining contenders.

### When is the next F1 race, and is Singapore a Sprint weekend?

The next race is the **Singapore Grand Prix on 11 October**, with track activity beginning on Friday, 9 October. It is a **Sprint weekend**: Sprint qualifying takes place on Friday, followed by the Sprint and Grand Prix qualifying on Saturday.

### Who won the last F1 race at Sepang?

Max Verstappen won the 2017 Malaysian Grand Prix for Red Bull, ahead of Lewis Hamilton and Daniel Ricciardo.

Motor car race

The **2017 Malaysian Grand Prix** (formally known as the **2017 Formula 1 Petronas Malaysia Grand Prix**)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Malaysian_Grand_Prix#cite_note-formal-4) was a [Formula One motor race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formula_One_racing) that was held on 1 October 2017 at the [Sepang International Circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sepang_International_Circuit) in [Selangor, Malaysia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selangor). The race marked the 37th running of the [Malaysian Grand Prix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysian_Grand_Prix), and the 19th time that the race had been run as a World Championship event, since the championship's inception in [1950](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1950_Formula_One_season), all World Championship events having been held at the Sepang International Circuit. [[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Malaysian_Grand_Prix#cite_note-5)

Hamilton's teammate [Valtteri Bottas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valtteri_Bottas) was third, a further 23 points behind. In the World Constructors' Championship, Mercedes held a lead of 102 points over Ferrari, with [Red Bull Racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Bull_Racing) a further 143 points behind in third place.

### Qualifying
[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2017_Malaysian_Grand_Prix&action=edit&section=5)]

Sebastian Vettel failed to set a time in Q1 as his replacement engine did not run properly meaning that he would start last on the grid. Championship leader Lewis Hamilton took pole position with a time of 1:30.076, ahead of Kimi Räikkönen and Max Verstappen. [[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Malaysian_Grand_Prix#cite_note-10)

### Race
[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2017_Malaysian_Grand_Prix&action=edit&section=6)]

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/Malaysia_GP_2017_Starting_Grid.jpg/250px-Malaysia_GP_2017_Starting_Grid.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Malaysia_GP_2017_Starting_Grid.jpg) Starting grid of the race[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/01/Max_Verstappen_overtaking_Lewis_Hamilton_2017_Malaysia_2.jpg/250px-Max_Verstappen_overtaking_Lewis_Hamilton_2017_Malaysia_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Max_Verstappen_overtaking_Lewis_Hamilton_2017_Malaysia_2.jpg) Verstappen overtakes Hamilton for the lead

Kimi Räikkönen pulled off the grid due to a power unit issue. Hamilton got off well with Ricciardo, Bottas and Verstappen behind. Verstappen overtook Hamilton for the lead on lap 4, and led until lap 28 when he pitted, leaving Ricciardo in the lead. Ricciardo then also pitted and Verstappen retook the lead. Coming into the last laps, Hamilton tried fighting back but Verstappen won comfortably to take his second win in his career, a year after his previous at the [2016 Spanish Grand Prix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Spanish_Grand_Prix).

Meanwhile, Vettel came back from last to 4th through the field, almost overtaking Ricciardo in third. [[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Malaysian_Grand_Prix#cite_note-11)

- F1 Full Results \| Max Verstappen wins chaotic Bahrain GP in Malaysia


Henry Eccles

Sun, October 4, 2026 at 10:20 AM UTC·

2 min read

**Max Verstappen** **has secured victory at the Bahrain GP in Malaysia, finishing ahead of** **Kimi Antonelli** **and** **Lewis Hamilton** **with a dominant display upon** **F1** **'s return to Sepang for the first time since 2017.**

Due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, fan favourite Sepang stepped in to host the Bahrain GP, originally scheduled for April, and has not disappointed in drama after nine years off the calendar.

Advertisement

As heavy rain pounded the track in the 30 minutes prior to the race, the Grand Prix was [unsurprisingly delayed](https://www.gpblog.com/en/breaking-news/bahrain-gp-officially-delayed-after-major-downpour-strikes-sepang), with Sepang known for its extreme and ever-changing conditions. Famously, in 2009 the race was abandoned after 33 of 56 laps, with Brawn GP's Jenson Button taking a half-point win on that occasion.

After 40 minutes, cars were making their way around, but the starting procedure had to be suspended after [complete chaos](https://www.gpblog.com/en/news/incredible-scenes-at-sepang-as-hamilton-and-several-drivers-suddenly-stop-on-track) under the formation lap, with the Red Flag brought out.

Hamilton, Esteban Ocon and Valtteri Bottas - each powered by Ferrari engines - had all stopped on track with suspected power unit troubles. Although Hamilton had been overtaken - and others lapped - amid his issues, the race got underway with the original starting grid.

And the chaos did not stop there, with the grid split between intermediate and slick tyres at race start. Hamilton, alongside those to take a gamble on slicks, once again fell to the back of the grid immediately, as Mercedes powered into the lead. Antonelli and Russell blasted to P1 and P2, respectively, ahead of Verstappen.

Advertisement

The Dutchman took little time to regain P2 from Russell, and was right behind Antonelli amid a Lap 9 Safety Car caused by Bottas' trip into the gravel. Upon the restart, a fantastic move from the four-time champion at the Turn 1 and 2 sequence saw him regain his lead.

Russell gained P2 from his teammate upon the restart, but on Lap 22, Antonelli was back ahead of the Briton. Verstappen, however, was now in the distance, building a gap of over eight seconds by halfway.

Hamilton, meanwhile, charged through the midfield in impressive fashion as he aimed to recover from Ferrari's [catastrophic tyre blunder.](https://www.gpblog.com/en/breaking-news/mercedes-stun-verstappen-at-the-start-as-hamilton-suffers-nightmare-getaway) After pushing back on Ferrari's calls to pit after the slow start, the Briton had made his way up to P5 by Lap 28 on older soft tyres.

More drama ensued after the Safety Car was brought out with nine laps remaining with Williams' Alex Albon suffering a gearbox issue. Russell was out of this race, stopping on the side of the track under the Safety Car after a suspected power unit failure.

A final five-lap showdown saw Verstappen blast into the distance from Antonelli, while Hamilton completed a remarkable recovery drive to take the final podium place from Red Bull's Hadjar.
